tools.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) is a critical infrastructure geospatial data repository that allows mission partners to access federally derived and acquired data within several critical infrastructure sectors, including agriculture, chemicals, communications, education, emergency services, energy, finances, transportation, and water.

**Data Access and Format:**
Data is available for download as CSV, KML, Shapefile, or File Geodatabase, and is accessible via web services via the Geospatial Information Infrastructure (GII).

**Access Requirements:**
Users (including federal, Tribal, state, local and territorial partners) who support a homeland security or homeland defense mission qualify for access. HIFLD Secure contains commercially licensed and FOUO (for official use only) data housed on the DHS Geospatial Information Infrastructure (GII). Access requires a GII account, a profile, and an approved Data Use Agreement (DUA).

**Public Data Portal:**
In August 2025, HIFLD Open, a public data portal managed by the U.S. Department was established, which would provide public access to certain HIFLD datasets, including the fiber optic cable network data.

For downloading the shapefile, you would need to access either HIFLD Open (for public data) or the HIFLD Secure system (if you have the required credentials for homeland security purposes).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about FCC Broadband Data Collection fiber availability shapefile downloads:

## Data Download Options

The availability data for fixed broadband services are available in a tabular comma separated value (CSV) format, while the mobile availability coverage maps are available in geographic information system (GIS) formats, such as shapefile.

## Where to Download

You can download availability and coverage information shown on the map by provider, for specific areas, or the nationwide data set. The official source is BroadbandMap.FCC.gov, which also has a dedicated data download section at broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download.

## Data Format for Fixed Broadband

It's important to note that the availability data for fixed broadband services are available in a tabular comma separated value (CSV) format, not shapefiles. The BDC requires fixed wireline and satellite providers to submit a list of locations or a polygon shapefile of their service territories by speeds, latency, and transmission technologies. However, the publicly available downloads appear to be primarily in CSV format for fixed broadband.

For more detailed information and to access the downloads, you can visit the FCC National Broadband Map website directly.

entries.description:
IMPORTANT: WebFetch WILL FAIL for authenticated or private URLs. Before using this tool, check if the URL points to an authenticated service (e.g. Google Docs, Confluence, Jira, GitHub). If so, look for a specialized MCP tool that provides authenticated access.
- Exception: claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}, including preview.claude.ai) ARE fetchable — WebFetch uses your claude.ai login. Use WebFetch for these, not curl or a headless browser (those return the SPA shell or a Cloudflare 403, not the content).

- Fetches content from a specified URL and processes it using an AI model
- Takes a URL and a prompt as input
- Fetches the URL content, converts HTML to markdown
- Processes the content with the prompt using a small, fast model
- Returns the model's response about the content
- Use this tool when you need to retrieve and analyze web content

Usage notes:
  - IMPORTANT: If an MCP-provided web fetch tool is available, prefer using that tool instead of this one, as it may have fewer restrictions.
  - The URL must be a fully-formed valid URL
  - HTTP URLs will be automatically upgraded to HTTPS
  - localhost and other hostnames without a dot are not supported; for a local server, use curl via Bash
  - The prompt should describe what information you want to extract from the page
  - This tool is read-only and does not modify any files
  - Results may be summarized if the content is very large
  - Includes a self-cleaning cache (entries expire after 15 minutes) for faster responses when repeatedly accessing the same URL
  - When a URL redirects to a different host, the tool will inform you and provide the redirect URL in a special format. You should then make a new WebFetch request with the redirect URL to fetch the content.
  - For GitHub URLs, prefer using the gh CLI via Bash instead (e.g., gh pr view, gh issue view, gh api).

CRITICAL REQUIREMENT - You MUST follow this:

  - In the Sources section, list all relevant URLs from the search results as markdown hyperlinks: [Title](URL)
  - This is MANDATORY - never skip including sources in your response

**OpenFiberMap**
OpenFiberMap aggregates open-licensed datasets (AfTerFibre, OFDS, PeeringDB, and others) into a single interactive globe, visualizing routes by capacity tier, operational status, and operator. Coverage is densest in Africa and select countries where structured open data exists, though geometries are approximate — many routes are digitized from public maps rather than authoritative records.

OFDS is a collection of datasets created from public maps of terrestrial fiber networks, available as GeoJSON files representing network nodes (Points of Presence) and network spans/links (line segments). content.content:
# OFDS Public Data Repository Summary

## Countries/Regions with Datasets

The repository contains fiber network data for 24 countries/regions:

Angola, Australia, Botswana, Brazil, Cameroon, Canada, Congo Republic, Costa Rica, Gabon, Georgia, Mozambique, Namibia, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Philippines, South Africa, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, and Zimbabwe.

**No United States dataset is present** in this collection.

## Data Format

Three formats are provided for each network:

1. **JSON**: "Full OFDS-compliant JSON (networks, nodes, spans)"
2. **GeoJSON (Nodes)**: Points of Presence represented as geographic points
3. **GeoJSON (Spans)**: Network connections represented as line segments

## How to Access

Data is housed in a GitHub repository organized by country and operator directories. Users can download files directly from the repository or access processed outputs including PMTiles artifacts and combined GeoJSON files hosted on Amazon S3.

## Important Note

"These maps are digitized from publicly available sources and are **approximations**, not authoritative" records—location data may be approximate rather than precise.

Angola, Australia, Botswana, Brazil, Cameroon, Canada, Congo Republic, Costa Rica, Gabon, Georgia, Mozambique, Namibia, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Philippines, South Africa, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, and Zimbabwe.

**No United States dataset is present** in this collection.

## Data Format

Three formats are provided for each network:

1. **JSON**: "Full OFDS-compliant JSON (networks, nodes, spans)"
2. **GeoJSON (Nodes)**: Points of Presence represented as geographic points
3. **GeoJSON (Spans)**: Network connections represented as line segments

## How to Access

Data is housed in a GitHub repository organized by country and operator directories. Users can download files directly from the repository or access processed outputs including PMTiles artifacts and combined GeoJSON files hosted on Amazon S3.

## Important Note

"These maps are digitized from publicly available sources and are **approximations**, not authoritative" records—location data may be approximate rather than precise.

content.text:
Good news and bad news on this. Let me lay out what I found.

**Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD) layer is power-only, confirmed.** I checked its actual attributes: `NAICS_DESC = "ELECTRIC BULK POWER TRANSMISSION AND CONTROL"`, a `VOLTAGE` field, owners like "ALABAMA POWER CO". Zero relation to data networks — that layer stays as-is.

**A true "all US data-carrying fiber networks" layer doesn't exist as a downloadable dataset — for the same reason Lumen only gives you an interactive map, not a download.** Carriers treat exact fiber routes as proprietary/security-sensitive info, and this isn't unique to Lumen:
- HIFLD (the government's infrastructure-data clearinghouse, same source as your power-lines layer) has never published a route-level nationwide fiber layer — it's excluded for the same critical-infrastructure-sensitivity reasons.
- The one open global fiber-mapping effort I found (OFDS/OpenFiberMap) has zero US coverage — 24 countries, US isn't one of them.
- OpenStreetMap's fiber tags exist but are too sparse in the US to be usable (not enough contributors map buried conduit).
- Your project already has `Internet2 Physical Routes` — that's real fiber route data, but it's one network (a research/education backbone), same "single company" problem as Lumen.

So there's no single clean source. Here are the realistic options, each a different tradeoff:

questions.question: Given there's no single authoritative multi-carrier fiber route dataset, which approach should the new data-network layer use?

options.label: FCC fiber availability (Recommended)
options.description: FCC Broadband Data Collection: real government data reported by every ISP nationwide, shows where fiber-based data service is available. Not exact conduit routes, but genuinely multi-carrier and comprehensive (all companies, not just one).

options.label: Likely fiber-corridor proxy
options.description: Add Interstate highways + active rail lines as a labeled 'likely fiber corridor' layer, since long-haul carriers overwhelmingly bury conduit along these rights-of-way. Route-shaped lines nationwide, but it's an inference, not verified placement — would be clearly labeled as such.

options.label: Verified networks only
options.description: Stick to networks with confirmed public route data: keep Internet2, and add other real ones I can find (e.g. ESnet, the Dept. of Energy's science network). Smaller and incomplete, but everything shown is 100% real, not inferred.

options.label: State broadband office data
options.description: Many states publish 'existing fiber infrastructure' GIS layers (compiled from ISPs for federal BEAD grant mapping) — most accurate option, but state-by-state, slower to assemble, and only covers states that publish it.

# FCC Broadband Data Collection Service

**Title:** FCC Broadband Data Collection December 2025 (Latest)

**Type:** Feature Service

**Description:** This geospatial dataset presents fixed broadband availability metrics across U.S. Census Blocks and hexagonal areas. It categorizes "Broadband Serviceable Locations (BSLs)" into three tiers: served (≥100/20 Mbps), underserved (25/3 to <100/20 Mbps), and unserved. The dataset includes transmission technology breakdowns and related tables listing ISP offerings by provider name and speed tier, facilitating analysis of broadband infrastructure gaps and BEAD program eligibility.

**REST Endpoint URL:** 
```
https://services8.arcgis.com/peDZJliSvYims39Q/arcgis/rest/services/FCC_Broadband_Data_Collection_December_2024_View/FeatureServer
```

**Additional Details:**
- Owner: Esri Policy Maps
- Coverage: December 2025 data
- Spatial Reference: Web Mercator (EPSG:3857)
- Public access with 338,451+ views
- Data sourced from the Federal Communications Commission

# FeatureServer Layers and Tables

## Layers (Feature Layers - Polygon Geometry)
- **ID 0**: States
- **ID 1**: Counties
- **ID 2**: Tracts
- **ID 3**: Block Groups
- **ID 4**: Blocks
- **ID 5**: "H3 Resolution 8"

## Tables
- **ID 6**: BDC Records for H3 Resolution 8
- **ID 7**: BDC Records for Blocks
- **ID 8**: BDC Records for Block Groups
- **ID 9**: BDC Records for Tracts
- **ID 10**: BDC Records for Counties
- **ID 11**: BDC Records for States

## Recommendation

**Layer ID 5 ("H3 Resolution 8")** is your best match. It provides hexagon-level geographic divisions suitable for US-wide mapping at an intermediate aggregation level—above block-level granularity but below county scale. This avoids both the millions-of-rows problem of block-level data and the coarseness of larger administrative boundaries.

Note: The document doesn't specify feature counts or fiber/technology field breakdowns, so you'll need to inspect the layer's schema to confirm it contains the broadband technology classifications you need.

# BDC Records for Counties - Table Structure

## Fields

| Name | Type | Alias |
|------|------|-------|
| OBJECTID | esriFieldTypeOID | OBJECTID |
| GEOID | esriFieldTypeString | Geographic Identifier |
| ProviderName | esriFieldTypeString | Provider Name |
| FRN | esriFieldTypeString | FCC Registration Number |
| Technology | esriFieldTypeSmallInteger | Transmission Technology |
| TotalBSLs | esriFieldTypeInteger | Total Broadband Serviceable Locations |
| UnservedBSLs | esriFieldTypeInteger | Unserved BSLs |
| UnderservedBSLs | esriFieldTypeInteger | Underserved BSLs |
| ServedBSLs | esriFieldTypeInteger | Served BSLs |

## Technology Field

The **Technology** field contains coded values identifying broadband type:
- Copper Wire (10), Cable (40), Fiber (50), Geostationary Satellite (60), Non-geostationary Satellite (61), Unlicensed Terrestrial Fixed Wireless (70), Licensed Terrestrial Fixed Wireless (71), Licensed-by-Rule Terrestrial Fixed Wireless (72), and Other (0)

## Relationship to Counties

The relationship "BDC records to Counties" uses:
- **Relationship ID**: 1
- **Key Field**: GEOID
- **Cardinality**: One-to-Many (one county to many BDC records)
- **Role**: Destination

## Location Coverage Metrics

Three integer fields provide location counts (not percentages):
- **UnservedBSLs** - unserved locations
- **UnderservedBSLs** - underserved locations  
- **ServedBSLs** - served locations

# US Fiber & Data Infrastructure Map — Data Sources & Methodology Log

Project file: `100_gqis_source.qgz`
Log created: 2026-09-21

This log records where every layer in the project came from, why it was built the way
it was, and what limitations to keep in mind when citing this map in the thesis.

## Current layers

### Submarine Cables (TeleGeography, all)
- **Submarine Cables** (729 features) — merged from 708 separate single-cable layers
  that were originally split across individual tables in `telegeography_cables_by_name.gpkg`
  (each cable was its own layer, tanking QGIS performance). Merged via
  `native:mergevectorlayers` into `telegeography_cables_merged.gpkg`, verified feature
  count matched (729 in, 729 out) before the original 708-table file was deleted.
  Styled with a data-defined stroke color pulled from each feature's own `color`
  attribute (the dataset's built-in per-cable color scheme).
  - **Backups made before the merge:** `100_gqis_source_backup_20260921_143340.qgz`,
    `telegeography_cables_by_name_backup_20260921_143340.gpkg`

### US Internal Fiber (Internet2 + PeeringDB)
- **Internet2 Physical Routes** (91 features) — real, traced physical fiber/leased
  routes of Internet2's US research & education backbone. Source: Internet2's own
  published network map (`internet2.edu/infrastructure/i2-network-map`), which is
  built with `qgis2web` and exposes its underlying GeoJSON directly
  (`Network_3.js`). Categorized by `key`: `fiber` (owned dark fiber, long-haul),
  `leased` (short metro-local circuits), `infrastructure` (one segment,
  Sunnyvale↔LA — likely shared partner-network capacity, exact meaning not
  documented by Internet2).
- **Internet2 Sites** (195 features) — Optical Sites, Packet Sites, NAREX
  Exchanges, Regional Exchanges, and Cloud Onramps, also from Internet2's
  published map data.
- **Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD)** (93,996 features) — real electric power
  transmission line geometry (69kV–765kV), clipped to CONUS. Source: HIFLD Next
  (`hifld.publicenvirodata.org`), the community-preserved successor to DHS's
  HIFLD Open portal (shut down August 2025). Styled by voltage class. Note: this
  is electric grid infrastructure, not a data/cable network — kept in the project
  as context (matches the style of NREL's US data infrastructure map), removed
  and restored once at the user's request.
- **Removed from this group:** *Internet2 NAREX Links* (schematic straight-line
  connections representing peering relationships with partner research networks,
  not real traced fiber paths — removed since it isn't an actual physical cable
  route). *Data Centers & Carrier Facilities (PeeringDB)* and *Equinix Data
  Centers* and *Notable Data Centers (Wikidata)* — superseded by the FracTracker-based
  Data Centers layer, see below.

### Data Centers (FracTracker, Operating)
- **Data Centers (Operating)** (447 features) — sourced entirely from the user's
  own spreadsheet, `Copy of Data_Centers_Database.xlsx`, compiled by **FracTracker
  Alliance** (an environmental-advocacy nonprofit; data collected via media
  monitoring, permits, FOIA requests, and crowdsourcing —
  see `fractracker.org/data-centers`). Filtered to rows where `status = Operating`
  **and** at least one `info_source` citation is populated (447 of 1,684 total
  rows in the spreadsheet; the rest are Proposed/Permitted/Cancelled/Suspended or
  uncited). Single uniform icon per the user's request (no source-based styling).
  - **Attribution requirement:** FracTracker's terms of service require citation
    wherever this data is used publicly: *"Data provided by FracTracker Alliance,
    accessed via https://www.fractracker.org/data-centers/"* — this is baked into
    the layer's metadata abstract, but **must also be included in any thesis
    figure or published map** using this layer.
  - Earlier iterations of this layer merged in PeeringDB (664), Equinix official
    addresses (73, scraped from equinix.com facility pages), and Wikidata (15
    notable facilities). This was later simplified to FracTracker-only per the
    user's request for one unified icon and one source.

### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.

## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)

A full nationwide dataset of *actual commercial long-haul fiber routes* does not
exist in any accessible open form. Investigated and ruled out:
- **HIFLD's historical "Long Haul Fiber" layer** — no longer exists anywhere in
  the HIFLD Next archive (confirmed by searching the full 400+ layer catalog).
- **InterTubes** (Durairajan et al., UW-Madison, SIGCOMM 2015) — the most
  credible academic long-haul fiber map exists, but is access-gated via IMPACT
  Cybertrust (DHS-affiliated), requiring an account and approved data request.
- **Internet Atlas** (same UW-Madison team) — project domain (`internetatlas.org`)
  no longer resolves; effectively dead.
- **NREL's own "US Data Infrastructure" map** — confirmed to be a flat image
  only; NREL's own write-up states fiber routes are "estimated" and the map
  "cannot be made available as an interactive web map due to the sensitive and
  proprietary nature of the data."
- **Carrier-published maps** (Lumen, Zayo, etc.) — schematic marketing diagrams
  (straight city-to-city lines), not real geometry; several are gated behind
  lead-generation forms.
- **Equinix's own interactive map data** — deliberately obfuscated/encoded
  client-side against bulk extraction; not attempted to reverse-engineer.
- **SEC 10-K filings** (Digital Realty) — Item 2/Schedule III property
  disclosures are legally required but only report **metro-level aggregates**
  ("Northern Virginia: 16 buildings"), not individual addresses.
- **OpenStreetMap Overpass API** — public instances were unreachable/overloaded
  for the entire session; not pursued further given US fiber-tagging coverage in
  OSM is sparse anyway.

## Key methodology notes for the thesis write-up

1. Any claim that this map shows "the fiber network" should be scoped precisely:
   it shows Internet2's real backbone + submarine cable landings + data center
   locations, **not** the commercial carrier long-haul backbone, which remains
   non-public.
2. Data center coverage is real and sourced, but not exhaustive — FracTracker's
   collection methodology is advocacy-driven (skews toward large/newsworthy
   facilities); smaller low-profile colocation buildings may be under-represented.
3. All removed layers still exist in `us_internal_fiber.gpkg` (their GeoPackage
   tables were never deleted, only unlinked from the project) — anything can be
   re-added if needed later.

### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.

### Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)
- **Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)** (3,234 features) — county-level
  fixed-broadband availability statistics from the FCC's Broadband Data Collection (BDC),
  pulled via Esri's public "FCC Broadband Data Collection December 2025" Feature Service
  (`services8.arcgis.com/.../FCC_Broadband_Data_Collection_December_2024_View`), which
  republishes FCC BDC data without requiring the paid CostQuest Broadband Serviceable
  Location Fabric. Exported to a local snapshot
  (`fcc_bdc_fiber_availability_by_county.gpkg`) rather than kept as a live service, for
  reproducibility. Added a computed field, `PctFiberCoverage = ServedBSLsFiber /
  TotalBSLs * 100`, and styled as a 5-class graduated choropleth (Blues ramp), placed
  beneath the point/line layers in draw order so it doesn't obscure them.
  - **What this is / isn't:** NOT traced fiber route geometry — it's every ISP's

# US Fiber & Data Infrastructure Map — Data Sources & Methodology Log

Project file: `100_gqis_source.qgz`
Log created: 2026-09-21

This log records where every layer in the project came from, why it was built the way
it was, and what limitations to keep in mind when citing this map in the thesis.

## Current layers

### Submarine Cables (TeleGeography, all)
- **Submarine Cables** (729 features) — merged from 708 separate single-cable layers
  that were originally split across individual tables in `telegeography_cables_by_name.gpkg`
  (each cable was its own layer, tanking QGIS performance). Merged via
  `native:mergevectorlayers` into `telegeography_cables_merged.gpkg`, verified feature
  count matched (729 in, 729 out) before the original 708-table file was deleted.
  Styled with a data-defined stroke color pulled from each feature's own `color`
  attribute (the dataset's built-in per-cable color scheme).
  - **Backups made before the merge:** `100_gqis_source_backup_20260921_143340.qgz`,
    `telegeography_cables_by_name_backup_20260921_143340.gpkg`

### US Internal Fiber (Internet2 + PeeringDB)
- **Internet2 Physical Routes** (91 features) — real, traced physical fiber/leased
  routes of Internet2's US research & education backbone. Source: Internet2's own
  published network map (`internet2.edu/infrastructure/i2-network-map`), which is
  built with `qgis2web` and exposes its underlying GeoJSON directly
  (`Network_3.js`). Categorized by `key`: `fiber` (owned dark fiber, long-haul),
  `leased` (short metro-local circuits), `infrastructure` (one segment,
  Sunnyvale↔LA — likely shared partner-network capacity, exact meaning not
  documented by Internet2).
- **Internet2 Sites** (195 features) — Optical Sites, Packet Sites, NAREX
  Exchanges, Regional Exchanges, and Cloud Onramps, also from Internet2's
  published map data.
- **Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD)** (93,996 features) — real electric power
  transmission line geometry (69kV–765kV), clipped to CONUS. Source: HIFLD Next
  (`hifld.publicenvirodata.org`), the community-preserved successor to DHS's
  HIFLD Open portal (shut down August 2025). Styled by voltage class. Note: this
  is electric grid infrastructure, not a data/cable network — kept in the project
  as context (matches the style of NREL's US data infrastructure map), removed
  and restored once at the user's request.
- **Removed from this group:** *Internet2 NAREX Links* (schematic straight-line
  connections representing peering relationships with partner research networks,
  not real traced fiber paths — removed since it isn't an actual physical cable
  route). *Data Centers & Carrier Facilities (PeeringDB)* and *Equinix Data
  Centers* and *Notable Data Centers (Wikidata)* — superseded by the FracTracker-based
  Data Centers layer, see below.

### Data Centers (FracTracker, Operating)
- **Data Centers (Operating)** (447 features) — sourced entirely from the user's
  own spreadsheet, `Copy of Data_Centers_Database.xlsx`, compiled by **FracTracker
  Alliance** (an environmental-advocacy nonprofit; data collected via media
  monitoring, permits, FOIA requests, and crowdsourcing —
  see `fractracker.org/data-centers`). Filtered to rows where `status = Operating`
  **and** at least one `info_source` citation is populated (447 of 1,684 total
  rows in the spreadsheet; the rest are Proposed/Permitted/Cancelled/Suspended or
  uncited). Single uniform icon per the user's request (no source-based styling).
  - **Attribution requirement:** FracTracker's terms of service require citation
    wherever this data is used publicly: *"Data provided by FracTracker Alliance,
    accessed via https://www.fractracker.org/data-centers/"* — this is baked into
    the layer's metadata abstract, but **must also be included in any thesis
    figure or published map** using this layer.
  - Earlier iterations of this layer merged in PeeringDB (664), Equinix official
    addresses (73, scraped from equinix.com facility pages), and Wikidata (15
    notable facilities). This was later simplified to FracTracker-only per the
    user's request for one unified icon and one source.

### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.

## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)

A full nationwide dataset of *actual commercial long-haul fiber routes* does not
exist in any accessible open form. Investigated and ruled out:
- **HIFLD's historical "Long Haul Fiber" layer** — no longer exists anywhere in
  the HIFLD Next archive (confirmed by searching the full 400+ layer catalog).
- **InterTubes** (Durairajan et al., UW-Madison, SIGCOMM 2015) — the most
  credible academic long-haul fiber map exists, but is access-gated via IMPACT
  Cybertrust (DHS-affiliated), requiring an account and approved data request.
- **Internet Atlas** (same UW-Madison team) — project domain (`internetatlas.org`)
  no longer resolves; effectively dead.
- **NREL's own "US Data Infrastructure" map** — confirmed to be a flat image
  only; NREL's own write-up states fiber routes are "estimated" and the map
  "cannot be made available as an interactive web map due to the sensitive and
  proprietary nature of the data."
- **Carrier-published maps** (Lumen, Zayo, etc.) — schematic marketing diagrams
  (straight city-to-city lines), not real geometry; several are gated behind
  lead-generation forms.
- **Equinix's own interactive map data** — deliberately obfuscated/encoded
  client-side against bulk extraction; not attempted to reverse-engineer.
- **SEC 10-K filings** (Digital Realty) — Item 2/Schedule III property
  disclosures are legally required but only report **metro-level aggregates**
  ("Northern Virginia: 16 buildings"), not individual addresses.
- **OpenStreetMap Overpass API** — public instances were unreachable/overloaded
  for the entire session; not pursued further given US fiber-tagging coverage in
  OSM is sparse anyway.

## Key methodology notes for the thesis write-up

1. Any claim that this map shows "the fiber network" should be scoped precisely:
   it shows Internet2's real backbone + submarine cable landings + data center
   locations, **not** the commercial carrier long-haul backbone, which remains
   non-public.
2. Data center coverage is real and sourced, but not exhaustive — FracTracker's
   collection methodology is advocacy-driven (skews toward large/newsworthy
   facilities); smaller low-profile colocation buildings may be under-represented.
3. All removed layers still exist in `us_internal_fiber.gpkg` (their GeoPackage
   tables were never deleted, only unlinked from the project) — anything can be
   re-added if needed later.

I opened Lumen's actual map page to check firsthand. It confirms exactly what your project's own methodology log already found — and adds a harder blocker:

> *"Lumen Network Maps are representative of our networks but in general terms. Exact locations and routes are subject to change... **No duplication permitted.**"*

Two separate problems, either one is disqualifying on its own:

1. **It's not real geometry.** Lumen states outright these are schematic/representative, not surveyed routes. Even if I extracted every coordinate perfectly, you'd get marketing-map approximations, not actual fiber paths — the same issue your log already flagged for Zayo and other carrier maps.
2. **"No duplication permitted" is an explicit legal restriction**, not just fine print. Scraping the underlying map data (even the schematic version) and reproducing it in your thesis project would violate Lumen's stated terms. I won't extract or copy data a source has explicitly prohibited reproducing, regardless of technical feasibility — this applies the same way whether it's one company's map or twelve.

So this dead-ends the same way it did in your original investigation, and going company-by-company (Zayo, AT&T, GTT, etc.) will hit the same two problems each time — they're standard industry practice for exactly the "no duplication" reason.

The two paths that could still get you real route-level geometry, neither of which I've pursued yet:

- **InterTubes** (Durairajan et al., SIGCOMM 2015) — the one credible academic long-haul fiber dataset, gated behind an IMPACT Cybertrust account + approved data request. I can't get this myself, but I can help you prepare that request if you want to pursue it.
- **State broadband office GIS data** — several states publish "existing fiber infrastructure" layers compiled from ISP submissions for BEAD federal grant mapping (multi-carrier, not schematic, real submitted data). Coverage varies by state and I haven't checked which states actually publish this yet.

Want me to check state broadband-office data availability, or hold here?

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding NTIA BEAD existing broadband infrastructure maps and data availability:

## Public Data Access

NTIA's NBAM has public data which is available on the NTIA Public Data site. However, the platform includes both publicly available and non-public data, with non-public data that may be business sensitive or have licensing restrictions, making NTIA's NBAM only available to state, tribal, and federal partners that have signed Joint Project Agreements or Memorandum of Understanding with NTIA.

## State-Specific BEAD Maps

Individual states are releasing their own BEAD data and maps. For example, California provides a Post-Challenge Process BEAD Map and Data webpage that represents the results of California's Broadband Equity Access and Deployment (BEAD) Challenge Process and identifies all BEAD-eligible Broadband Serviceable Locations in California.

## Licensing Requirements for GIS Data

An important restriction to note: Under the terms of CostQuest Associates licensing, the office cannot allow downloads of the fabric used to generate maps or otherwise make them available to unlicensed third parties, and parties interested in analyzing this data using their internal GIS resources will need to apply for a license at apps.costquest.com/NTIArequest.

For detailed state-specific BEAD information, you'll want to check your state's broadband office website, as most states are publishing their own BEAD-related maps and eligibility data.

# Broadband Data and Analytics Resources

Based on the webpage content, here are the consolidated resources mentioned:

## National-Level Platforms

**NTIA Broadband Analytics and Monitoring (NBAM)**
- Primary platform: https://nbam.ntia.gov/
- Described as "a secure GIS platform and data analytics tool for the visualization and comparison of federal, state, and commercially available data sets"
- Includes public data accessible via the NTIA Public Data site

**NTIA Public GIS Data**
- Located at: https://nbam.ntia.gov/pages/open-data
- Contains dashboards and geospatial data for multiple NTIA programs

## Important Limitations

The webpage does **not** provide:
- Direct links to individual state-by-state data portals
- Consolidated directory of state broadband office GIS data
- Maps specifically showing fiber infrastructure route lines (the page notes that older applications focused on "broadband availability" rather than infrastructure routes)

## Related Resource

The **FCC National Broadband Map** (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/home) is mentioned as a separate resource providing broadband serviceable location data, though it is not a state office directory.

For direct state data access, the page indicates users must "contact NTIA" at the provided email address.

Georgia has published a Broadband Availability Map as a new tool that will bring more transparency about the internet marketplace and clarify which Georgia households do not have access to high-speed internet. The Georgia Broadband Map project represents a location-level methodology that precisely maps the availability of broadband services to every home and business in the State, which includes all 159 counties.

The State's map is based on location-specific data, which is a more accurate reflection of which Georgia households have high-speed internet available via wireline, such as fiber optic cable.

For accessing map data, the FCC provides downloads of their Broadband Data Collection effort from their FCC National Broadband Map at https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download. The Georgia Broadband Program's website at broadband.georgia.gov offers the interactive maps and additional resources for broadband availability information throughout the state.

However, the search results do not provide specific information about shapefile downloads or GIS-ready data in that format for Georgia's broadband infrastructure. You may want to contact the Georgia Technology Authority or check the broadband.georgia.gov website directly for GIS data availability.

The Office of Broadband Development at the Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED) has contracted with Connected Nation to create broadband availability maps.

### Data Access Points

1. **Minnesota Geospatial Commons**: The Minnesota broadband interactive map provides tools and layers to examine broadband availability at your address, town, township, county, tribal nation, etc. The data is available at gisdata.mn.gov with downloads available in CSV, KML, Zip, GeoJSON, GeoTIFF or PNG formats, with API links for GeoServices, WMS, and WFS.

3. **DEED Maps and Data Webpage**: Additional broadband products including static maps and statistical charts are available through DEED's official broadband maps page.

### Important Note on Fiber Route Maps

## Primary Data Sources

The California State Geoportal allows you to discover, analyze and download data in multiple formats including CSV, KML, Zip, GeoJSON, and GeoTIFF.

There is a GIS layer representing the statewide middle-mile broadband network infrastructure in California with version tracking, available at the California State Geoportal.

## Main Resources

1. **California State Geoportal**: https://gis.data.ca.gov/search?categories=/categories/mmbi+website/public+item&collection=dataset

2. **MMBI Statewide Network Versions Download**: https://gis.data.ca.gov/datasets/cammbi::mmbi-statewide-network-versions-download-vw

3. **ArcGIS Hub - Statewide Middle-Mile Network Map**: https://site-cammbi.hub.arcgis.com/pages/statewide-middle-mile-network-map - Where you can download in CSV, KML, Zip, GeoJSON formats and find API links for GeoServices, WMS, and WFS

4. **CPUC Data & Analysis Portal**: https://middle-mile-broadband-initiative.cdt.ca.gov/pages/data-and-analysis

5. **Broadband for All Portal**: https://broadbandforall.cdt.ca.gov/middle-mile-broadband-initiative/statewide-middle-mile-network/

The Project Status Interactive Network Map visualizes the current progress of network route miles across various statuses: pre-construction, installation, and ready-to-connect, with the map updated the last Monday of every month.

# MMBI Statewide Network Layer Analysis

**Geometry Type:** Line geometry (polyline) - confirmed as route/network data

**Field Names & Aliases:**
- OBJECTID (FID)
- Version_MonthYear
- Process_Status (display field)
- Version
- Version_Date
- Version_Network

**Usage/Licensing:**
- Copyright: "copyright Python API guide"
- Description: "Updated using ArcGIS Python API"

**Key Observations:**
This is a polyline feature layer representing a statewide network with version tracking. The layer includes a `Process_Status` field for workflow management and `Version_MonthYear` for temporal differentiation (January 2024 and October 2023 versions documented). A `definitionQuery` filters to exclude certain process statuses. No dedicated mileage field is explicitly listed, though the geometry properties reference a "Shape__Length" field in meters for spatial measurements.

input.new_string:
### CA Middle-Mile Fiber Network (CDT/MMBI, real routes)
- **CA Middle-Mile Fiber Network** (1 multipart feature, California only) — this is the
  first *actual traced fiber route geometry* in the project for a commercial/public
  long-haul network beyond Internet2. Source: California's Middle-Mile Broadband
  Initiative (state-funded open-access fiber build, run by the CA Department of
  Technology), published as a versioned Feature Service
  (`services6.arcgis.com/sAv98EYUZbLCVPW0/.../MMBI_Statewide_Network_Versions_Download_vw`)
  with one snapshot polyline per month since January 2024. Pulled the latest snapshot
  (**August 2026**) and exported to a local file,
  `ca_middle_mile_fiber_network_2026-08.gpkg`, rather than keeping the live service link.
  - **Why this is real and Lumen's isn't:** this is state government infrastructure
    (public funds, public accountability), not a carrier's marketing map — no "no
    duplication" restriction, no "representative, not exact" disclaimer. It's also why
    it's scoped to one state: this kind of genuinely public, real-geometry fiber data
    only exists where a state (or other public entity) built/funded the network itself.
  - **Scope limitation:** California only. This does not generalize automatically —
    other states would each need to be checked individually for an equivalent
    state-funded middle-mile program with public GIS data (many states' broadband
    offices publish availability data like the FCC BDC layer above, but not
    necessarily real route geometry — e.g. Minnesota's broadband GIS hub was checked
    and only has availability/coverage data, not route lines).
  - Lumen's own published network map (`lumen.com/en-us/resources/network-maps.html`)
    was checked directly (not just recalled from the earlier investigation) and confirmed
    disqualified on two independent grounds: (1) self-described as "representative...
    in general terms," not exact routes, and (2) explicitly states "No duplication
    permitted" — ruling out both automated extraction and manual tracing of their map.

## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)

# US Fiber & Data Infrastructure Map — Data Sources & Methodology Log

Project file: `100_gqis_source.qgz`
Log created: 2026-09-21

This log records where every layer in the project came from, why it was built the way
it was, and what limitations to keep in mind when citing this map in the thesis.

## Current layers

### Submarine Cables (TeleGeography, all)
- **Submarine Cables** (729 features) — merged from 708 separate single-cable layers
  that were originally split across individual tables in `telegeography_cables_by_name.gpkg`
  (each cable was its own layer, tanking QGIS performance). Merged via
  `native:mergevectorlayers` into `telegeography_cables_merged.gpkg`, verified feature
  count matched (729 in, 729 out) before the original 708-table file was deleted.
  Styled with a data-defined stroke color pulled from each feature's own `color`
  attribute (the dataset's built-in per-cable color scheme).
  - **Backups made before the merge:** `100_gqis_source_backup_20260921_143340.qgz`,
    `telegeography_cables_by_name_backup_20260921_143340.gpkg`

### US Internal Fiber (Internet2 + PeeringDB)
- **Internet2 Physical Routes** (91 features) — real, traced physical fiber/leased
  routes of Internet2's US research & education backbone. Source: Internet2's own
  published network map (`internet2.edu/infrastructure/i2-network-map`), which is
  built with `qgis2web` and exposes its underlying GeoJSON directly
  (`Network_3.js`). Categorized by `key`: `fiber` (owned dark fiber, long-haul),
  `leased` (short metro-local circuits), `infrastructure` (one segment,
  Sunnyvale↔LA — likely shared partner-network capacity, exact meaning not
  documented by Internet2).
- **Internet2 Sites** (195 features) — Optical Sites, Packet Sites, NAREX
  Exchanges, Regional Exchanges, and Cloud Onramps, also from Internet2's
  published map data.
- **Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD)** (93,996 features) — real electric power
  transmission line geometry (69kV–765kV), clipped to CONUS. Source: HIFLD Next
  (`hifld.publicenvirodata.org`), the community-preserved successor to DHS's
  HIFLD Open portal (shut down August 2025). Styled by voltage class. Note: this
  is electric grid infrastructure, not a data/cable network — kept in the project
  as context (matches the style of NREL's US data infrastructure map), removed
  and restored once at the user's request.
- **Removed from this group:** *Internet2 NAREX Links* (schematic straight-line
  connections representing peering relationships with partner research networks,
  not real traced fiber paths — removed since it isn't an actual physical cable
  route). *Data Centers & Carrier Facilities (PeeringDB)* and *Equinix Data
  Centers* and *Notable Data Centers (Wikidata)* — superseded by the FracTracker-based
  Data Centers layer, see below.

### Data Centers (FracTracker, Operating)
- **Data Centers (Operating)** (447 features) — sourced entirely from the user's
  own spreadsheet, `Copy of Data_Centers_Database.xlsx`, compiled by **FracTracker
  Alliance** (an environmental-advocacy nonprofit; data collected via media
  monitoring, permits, FOIA requests, and crowdsourcing —
  see `fractracker.org/data-centers`). Filtered to rows where `status = Operating`
  **and** at least one `info_source` citation is populated (447 of 1,684 total
  rows in the spreadsheet; the rest are Proposed/Permitted/Cancelled/Suspended or
  uncited). Single uniform icon per the user's request (no source-based styling).
  - **Attribution requirement:** FracTracker's terms of service require citation
    wherever this data is used publicly: *"Data provided by FracTracker Alliance,
    accessed via https://www.fractracker.org/data-centers/"* — this is baked into
    the layer's metadata abstract, but **must also be included in any thesis
    figure or published map** using this layer.
  - Earlier iterations of this layer merged in PeeringDB (664), Equinix official
    addresses (73, scraped from equinix.com facility pages), and Wikidata (15
    notable facilities). This was later simplified to FracTracker-only per the
    user's request for one unified icon and one source.

### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.

### Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)
- **Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)** (3,234 features) — county-level
  fixed-broadband availability statistics from the FCC's Broadband Data Collection (BDC),
  pulled via Esri's public "FCC Broadband Data Collection December 2025" Feature Service
  (`services8.arcgis.com/.../FCC_Broadband_Data_Collection_December_2024_View`), which
  republishes FCC BDC data without requiring the paid CostQuest Broadband Serviceable
  Location Fabric. Exported to a local snapshot
  (`fcc_bdc_fiber_availability_by_county.gpkg`) rather than kept as a live service, for
  reproducibility. Added a computed field, `PctFiberCoverage = ServedBSLsFiber /
  TotalBSLs * 100`, and styled as a 5-class graduated choropleth (Blues ramp), placed
  beneath the point/line layers in draw order so it doesn't obscure them.
  - **What this is / isn't:** NOT traced fiber route geometry — it's every ISP's
    self-reported service availability, aggregated to the county polygon and summed
    across every provider reporting fiber (technology code 50) to the FCC. It answers
    "how much of this county can get fiber-based broadband, from any provider" — the
    multi-carrier counterpart the project was missing (Internet2 above is one network's
    real routes; this is every reporting ISP — Lumen, AT&T, Verizon, etc. included — but
    as availability stats, not physical routes). The source table also carries
    `UniqueProvidersFiber` (count of distinct fiber ISPs per county, kept but not used
    for styling) if that's useful later.
  - This is a different FCC data product (regulatory availability reporting) from the
    route-level "Long Haul Fiber" datasets ruled out below — it wasn't part of that
    earlier investigation.

## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)

A full nationwide dataset of *actual commercial long-haul fiber routes* does not
exist in any accessible open form. Investigated and ruled out:
- **HIFLD's historical "Long Haul Fiber" layer** — no longer exists anywhere in
  the HIFLD Next archive (confirmed by searching the full 400+ layer catalog).
- **InterTubes** (Durairajan et al., UW-Madison, SIGCOMM 2015) — the most
  credible academic long-haul fiber map exists, but is access-gated via IMPACT
  Cybertrust (DHS-affiliated), requiring an account and approved data request.
- **Internet Atlas** (same UW-Madison team) — project domain (`internetatlas.org`)
  no longer resolves; effectively dead.
- **NREL's own "US Data Infrastructure" map** — confirmed to be a flat image
  only; NREL's own write-up states fiber routes are "estimated" and the map
  "cannot be made available as an interactive web map due to the sensitive and
  proprietary nature of the data."
- **Carrier-published maps** (Lumen, Zayo, etc.) — schematic marketing diagrams
  (straight city-to-city lines), not real geometry; several are gated behind
  lead-generation forms.
- **Equinix's own interactive map data** — deliberately obfuscated/encoded
  client-side against bulk extraction; not attempted to reverse-engineer.
- **SEC 10-K filings** (Digital Realty) — Item 2/Schedule III property
  disclosures are legally required but only report **metro-level aggregates**
  ("Northern Virginia: 16 buildings"), not individual addresses.
- **OpenStreetMap Overpass API** — public instances were unreachable/overloaded
  for the entire session; not pursued further given US fiber-tagging coverage in
  OSM is sparse anyway.

## Key methodology notes for the thesis write-up

1. Any claim that this map shows "the fiber network" should be scoped precisely:
   it shows Internet2's real backbone + submarine cable landings + data center
   locations, **not** the commercial carrier long-haul backbone, which remains
   non-public. The FCC BDC county layer adds real multi-carrier coverage, but as
   aggregated availability statistics, not route geometry — don't conflate the two
   when writing about "the data network" in the thesis.
2. Data center coverage is real and sourced, but not exhaustive — FracTracker's
   collection methodology is advocacy-driven (skews toward large/newsworthy
   facilities); smaller low-profile colocation buildings may be under-represented.
3. All removed layers still exist in `us_internal_fiber.gpkg` (their GeoPackage
   tables were never deleted, only unlinked from the project) — anything can be
   re-added if needed later.

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__computer_batch
entries.description: Execute a sequence of actions in ONE tool call. Each individual tool call requires a model→API round trip (seconds); batching a predictable sequence eliminates all but one. Use this whenever you can predict the outcome of several actions ahead — e.g. click a field, type into it, press Return. Actions execute sequentially and stop on the first error. The frontmost application must be in the session allowlist at the time of this call, or this tool returns an error and does nothing. The frontmost check runs before EACH action inside the batch — if an action opens a non-allowed app, the next action's gate fires and the batch stops there. Screenshot and zoom actions are allowed and their images are returned interleaved with the per-action outputs. Coordinates you write in THIS batch — clicks AND zoom regions — always refer to the full-screen screenshot taken BEFORE this call, never to a zoom and never to a mid-batch screenshot. After the batch returns, the most recent full screenshot it produced becomes the new coordinate reference for your next call.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): Rectangle to zoom into. For zoom only. Coordinate space: the full-screen screenshot taken BEFORE this batch (never a mid-batch screenshot, never a prior zoom).

scale.description: For screenshot/zoom only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

start_coordinate.description: (x, y) drag start — left_click_drag only. Omit to drag from current cursor.

text.description: For type: the text. For key/hold_key: the chord string. For click/scroll: modifier keys to hold.

save_to_disk.description: Save the images produced by any screenshot/zoom actions in this batch to disk so they can be attached to a message for the user. The saved path(s) are returned in the result. Only set this when you intend to share the image(s) — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__teach_batch
entries.description: Queue multiple teach steps in one tool call. Parallels computer_batch: N steps → one model↔API round trip instead of N. Each step still shows a tooltip and waits for the user's Next click, but YOU aren't waiting for a round trip between steps. You can call teach_batch multiple times in one tour — treat each batch as one predictable SEGMENT (typically: all the steps on one page). The returned screenshot shows the state after the batch's final actions; anchor the NEXT teach_batch against it. WITHIN a batch, all anchors and click coordinates refer to the PRE-BATCH screenshot (same invariant as computer_batch) — for steps 2+ in a batch, either omit anchor (centered tooltip) or target elements you know won't have moved. Good pattern: batch 5 tooltips on page A (last step navigates) → read returned screenshot → batch 3 tooltips on page B → done. Returns {exited:true, stepsCompleted:N} if the user clicks Exit — do NOT call again after that; {stepsCompleted, stepFailed, ...} if an action errors mid-batch; otherwise {stepsCompleted, results:[...]} plus a final screenshot. Fall back to individual teach_step calls when you need to react to each intermediate screenshot.

next_preview.description: One line describing exactly what will happen when the user clicks Next. Example: "Next: I'll click Create Bucket and type the name." Shown below the explanation in a smaller font.

Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

text.description: For type: the text. For key/hold_key: the chord string. For click/scroll: modifier keys to hold.

actions.description: Actions to execute when the user clicks Next. Same item schema as computer_batch.actions. Empty array is valid for purely explanatory steps. Actions run sequentially and stop on first error.

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__teach_step
entries.description: Show one guided-tour tooltip and wait for the user to click Next. On Next, execute the actions, take a fresh screenshot, and return both — you do NOT need a separate screenshot call between steps. The returned image shows the state after your actions ran; anchor the next teach_step against it. IMPORTANT — the user only sees the tooltip during teach mode. Put ALL narration in `explanation`. Text you emit outside teach_step calls is NOT visible until teach mode ends. Pack as many actions as possible into each step's `actions` array — the user waits through the whole round trip between clicks, so one step that fills a form beats five steps that fill one field each. Returns {exited:true} if the user clicks Exit — do not call teach_step again after that. Take an initial screenshot before your FIRST teach_step to anchor it.

explanation.description: Tooltip body text. Explain what the user is looking at and why it matters. This is the ONLY place the user sees your words — be complete but concise.

next_preview.description: One line describing exactly what will happen when the user clicks Next. Example: "Next: I'll click Create Bucket and type the name." Shown below the explanation in a smaller font.

anchor.description: (x, y) — where the tooltip arrow points. Horizontal pixel position read directly from the most recent screenshot image, measured from the left edge. The server handles all scaling. Omit to center the tooltip with no arrow (for general-context steps).

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): Rectangle to zoom into. For zoom only. Coordinate space: the full-screen screenshot taken BEFORE this batch (never a mid-batch screenshot, never a prior zoom).

scale.description: For screenshot/zoom only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

start_coordinate.description: (x, y) drag start — left_click_drag only. Omit to drag from current cursor.

text.description: For type: the text. For key/hold_key: the chord string. For click/scroll: modifier keys to hold.

actions.description: Actions to execute when the user clicks Next. Same item schema as computer_batch.actions. Empty array is valid for purely explanatory steps. Actions run sequentially and stop on first error.

coordinate.description: (x, y): Horizontal pixel position read directly from the most recent screenshot image, measured from the left edge. The server handles all scaling.

text.description: Modifier keys to hold during the click (e.g. "shift", "ctrl+shift"). Supports the same syntax as the key tool.

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__type

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__wait

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__write_clipboard

input.description: Research states A-P for real fiber route data
input.prompt:
I'm helping build a QGIS map of US data/fiber infrastructure for a thesis project. We already have real traced fiber route geometry for two sources: Internet2 (national R&E backbone, from their published qgis2web GeoJSON) and California's Middle-Mile Broadband Initiative (CA Dept. of Technology's state-funded open-access fiber build — found via `https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/search?q=<title>&f=json` locating its ArcGIS Feature Service, confirmed `esriGeometryPolyline`, one snapshot per month).

We explicitly do NOT want:
- Carrier marketing maps (Lumen, Zayo, AT&T, etc.) — these are schematic ("representative... in general terms"), not real geometry, and typically carry "no duplication permitted" terms that rule out even manual tracing. Do not include these as findings.
- Broadband "availability" data — points or polygons showing where service *could* be gotten (FCC BDC, most state broadband-office maps). We already have this nationwide as a county choropleth. Only real physical ROUTE LINES count as a finding here.

Your job: for each of these 16 states — Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky — determine whether a real, publicly downloadable fiber/telecom ROUTE LINE dataset exists (not availability, not carrier marketing). Check these angles per state, roughly in this order, and don't over-invest — 3-5 targeted web searches per state is plenty; if nothing turns up, note it and move to the next state:

1. **State-funded middle-mile / open-access broadband build** (the CA MMBI pattern) — search "<state> middle mile broadband network map GIS data", "<state> broadband office existing infrastructure map download". Some states (e.g. via BEAD or older programs) built or are building their own fiber and publish it.
2. **State/regional Research & Education Network (REN)** — nearly every state has one of these (e.g. MOREnet in Missouri, OARnet in Ohio, KanREN in Kansas, LEARN in Texas, MCNC in North Carolina, OneNet in Oklahoma). These are nonprofit/state-chartered, non-commercial, and often publish real network maps like Internet2 does. Check "The Quilt" (thequilt.net), a coalition/directory of these regional networks, to identify each assigned state's REN, then check if that REN publishes a real map with underlying geodata (look for qgis2web-style embedded GeoJSON/JS files, an ArcGIS Feature Service, or a KMZ/GeoJSON download — same technique as Internet2).
3. **State DOT (Department of Transportation) fiber/conduit inventory** — some state DOTs publish GIS layers of fiber conduit along highway rights-of-way (built for permitting/utility coordination, e.g. dark fiber leasing programs). Search "<state> DOT fiber optic conduit GIS map".

For any ArcGIS-based source you find (Hub page, dashboard, etc.), use the technique that worked for CA: query `https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/search?q=<exact title or keywords>&f=json` to find the underlying Feature/Map Service URL directly, then fetch `<service_url>/<layer index>?f=json` to confirm `geometryType` is `esriGeometryPolyline` (a line layer) before counting it as a real finding — don't just report a webpage that *shows* a map without confirming there's an actual downloadable/queryable line layer behind it.

Report back a compact table, one row per state:
| State | Result (FOUND/NOT FOUND) | Source name & agency | Data URL (REST service or direct download) | Confirmed geometry type | Notes/license caveats |

Keep notes on NOT FOUND states to one short phrase (e.g. "broadband office only has availability polygons; no REN with public geodata found"). Don't write long prose — I need this table to decide which states get added to the actual QGIS project. Under 600 words total.

input.new_string:
### State & Regional Fiber Networks (real routes, verified) — 13 sources
- Following the CA MMBI precedent, ran a systematic state-by-state search (all 50 states)
  for real, publicly downloadable fiber ROUTE LINE data — not availability data, not
  carrier marketing maps. Checked three angles per state: (1) state-funded middle-mile/
  open-access builds, (2) state/regional Research & Education Networks (RENs — the same
  category Internet2 belongs to; coordinated nationally via "The Quilt"), (3) state DOT
  fiber/conduit inventories (built for highway permitting, a source type not previously
  considered). **13 states turned up real, verified polyline data.** Method for each: found
  a lead via web search, then used `https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/search?q=<title>&f=json`
  to locate the underlying ArcGIS Feature/Map Service directly, confirmed
  `esriGeometryPolyline` on the specific layer index, then loaded it into QGIS and checked
  extent + sample attributes actually made sense for that state/agency (not just took the
  metadata's word for it) before exporting to a local `.gpkg` snapshot. One file per state,
  named `<state>_fiber_network.gpkg`, all grouped together and given a uniform single-symbol
  style so they read as one visual category distinct from Internet2 and the CA layer.
  - **Alaska** (48 features) — AK Dept. of Natural Resources, compiled fiber cable
    alignments from infrastructure easement permit filings (EPF).
  - **Arizona** (54 features) — ADOT's own highway fiber conduit measurements (named by
    route, e.g. "101 EB (I-17 to Pima)").
  - **Illinois — IDOT District 4 only** (37 features) — traffic-signal interconnect fiber
    links, Peoria region only, not statewide.
  - **Kentucky** (9,596 features) — KentuckyWired, the state's own open-access middle-mile
    network (KY Transportation Cabinet). Source had 7 sublayers split by install type
    (Aerial/Underground) × status (Construction Complete/Permit Approved/Permit in
    Review) + a Third-Party Fiber layer; merged the 5 non-empty ones via
    `native:mergevectorlayers` (the 2 "Permit in Review" sublayers were empty).
  - **Maine** (16 features) — MOOSENet, Maine Connectivity Authority's state-funded
    open-access middle-mile.
  - **Nebraska** (277 features) — Network Nebraska, state OCIO-run fiber circuits.
  - **Nevada** (5,215 features) — HSNV (High Speed Nevada) Middle Mile, Governor's Office
    of Science, Innovation & Technology — tracks the state's own permitted/funded build
    segments (some built by contracted carriers like Zayo along I-80/US-93, but this is
    the state's construction-status tracking, not a scrape of the carrier's own map).
  - **New York — Southern Tier only** (11 features) — Southern Tier Network, a regional
    planning board's middle-mile build covering 5 counties, not statewide (NYSERNet, the
    statewide REN, only publishes a static image).
  - **North Carolina** (111 features) — MCNC, operator of NCREN; backbone segments dated
    back to a 2010–2013 BTOP federal stimulus build-out.
  - **Rhode Island** (638 features) — OSHEAN (the state's REN) network, via RI Commerce
    Corp's Broadband Office. Sourced from a KMZ audit file (route names like
    "Boston - Providence" with `length_miles`); the accompanying 2-feature "Middle Mile"
    summary layer was skipped as a redundant, coarser duplicate of the same info.
  - **Utah** (44,942 features) — UDOT's own fiber conduit inventory (via Horrocks
    Engineering, UDOT's GIS contractor). Very granular — individual conduit segments,
    not just corridors.
  - **Virginia — Southside only** (2,504 features) — Mid-Atlantic Broadband Communities
    Corp (MBC), an open-access middle-mile network covering Southside Virginia, not
    statewide.
  - **Washington** (33,398 features) — NoaNet (Northwest Open Access Network), an
    open-access network built by member Public Utility Districts (Franklin PUD, Okanogan
    County PUD, etc.) — publicly owned, updated quarterly per the source metadata.
  - **Maryland — checked but unconfirmed**: a promising lead (One Maryland Broadband
    Network / OMBN backbone, `geodata.md.gov`) returned HTTP 503 (service down) on two
    separate attempts. Worth retrying later; not added.
  - **States checked with no real route-line data found** (only static map images/PDFs,
    availability-only data, or middle-mile builds still under construction with nothing
    public yet): Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia,
    Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts (only a single
    submarine-cable arc, redundant with the existing Submarine Cables layer — skipped),
    Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, North
    Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania (an unofficial personal re-upload of
    KINBER/PennREN data exists but has unverifiable provenance — not used), South
    Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont (has a line-geometry dataset, but it
    turned out to be E911 road centerlines snapped to *provider-reported availability* —
    availability data disguised as routes — correctly excluded), West Virginia, Wisconsin,
    Wyoming.
  - **Two things this confirms about Lumen and other carrier maps, independent of the
    earlier check:** every real dataset found here is government/nonprofit-published
    (state DOTs, RENs, public utility districts) — none is a commercial carrier's own
    network map. That's the actual pattern: real public route geometry exists only where
    a public entity built or tracks the infrastructure itself, never from a carrier
    publishing its own competitive network map.

## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)

## Overview

FiberLocator operates as an online fiber mapping database. It is a CCMI business and serves as a comprehensive platform for telecommunications and data center information.

## Purpose and Functionality

FiberLocator provides users with a full understanding of the fiber providers within a given area, between two points or at a single location. The goal of fiber locator tools is to help telecom professionals compile data on their own fiber assets, partner assets, competitor assets, and broader market intelligence in one place.

## Database Content

FiberLocator is a rapidly growing, centralized database that catalogs hundreds of alternative access fiber providers as well as thousands of data centers and hundreds of thousands of lit buildings. It comprises data from hundreds of CLECs and facilities-based carriers, as well as hundreds of thousands of lit buildings and data centers.

## Target Users

Those in network planning, procurement or related functions such as commercial real estate or business intelligence can benefit from researching telecom and colocation information. IT professionals are turning to the FiberLocator suite of solutions to research, plan, design and deploy high capacity optical networks as well as data centers.

## Pricing

Subscriptions to FiberLocator are available starting at $4,500/year on a 12-month minimum term for the first seat.

content.content:
# FiberLocator Data Sourcing

**Primary Method: Direct Licensing from Carriers**

FiberLocator sources data directly from telecom carriers and network providers rather than scraping or crowdsourcing. The company states it partners with "carriers, data center operators, and infrastructure providers" who "provide their fiber routes and on-net building lists straight to FiberLocator."

**Data Characteristics: Current and Verified**

The data is described as precise and continuously validated. FiberLocator emphasizes that users access "data that reflects today's network reality" through "direct relationships, continuous validation, and a commitment to quality." Their team conducts ongoing audits and "validate[s] carrier-provided updates before publishing" them.

**Contrast with Competitors**

The page distinguishes FiberLocator's approach from competitors who "aggregate data from publicly accessible sources" like regulatory filings and construction permits—sources that are only "refreshed...once or twice a year" and often contain "incomplete coverage."

**Key Differentiator**

FiberLocator positions its direct carrier partnerships as enabling faster updates when "carriers expand or modify their networks, they send those updates directly to our team," minimizing lag time compared to public-source reliant competitors.

content.text:
A quick correction on framing first: this data isn't *classified* in the government-secrets sense — it's proprietary/commercially sensitive (owned by private carriers, or protected as critical infrastructure by policy, not by a security clearance regime). That distinction matters because it changes what's actually obtainable. Real workarounds researchers use for exactly this problem, roughly in order of how tractable they'd be for you:

**1. Regulatory/permit records (this is literally why your 13 state layers exist)**
Every source I found this session came from a state making its own infrastructure legible for a *non-mapping* reason: DOT permit tracking, construction status dashboards, federal grant compliance (BTOP, BEAD). The generalizable move: for states that came up empty, a direct public-records request (FOIA-equivalent — most states call it a "public records act request") to the DOT or broadband office asking specifically for "GIS shapefile of permitted fiber conduit" often surfaces data that exists internally but was never put on an open-data portal. Costs time (weeks), not money.

**2. Right-of-way inference / least-cost-path modeling**
This is the actual published-academic method (it's what InterTubes did, since even *they* couldn't get real routes everywhere) — fiber overwhelmingly follows existing legal rights-of-way because burying new conduit off an existing easement is expensive and requires new land agreements. So: take known endpoints (data centers, POPs, cable landing stations — you already have these) and known corridors (interstates, active rail, your power transmission layer), and compute a least-cost path between endpoints constrained to those corridors. This produces a *modeled, labeled-as-inferred* route layer, not a claim of real geometry — intellectually honest, reproducible, and it's a real GIS technique (QGIS has native least-cost-path tools) rather than guessing.

**3. OSINT / physical ground-truthing**
Buried fiber legally requires posted warning markers at road/rail crossings and periodic intervals (yellow "buried fiber optic cable" signs) — visible in Street View and satellite imagery. Aerial fiber on utility poles is visually distinguishable too. This is how some of the academic literature ground-truths inferred routes at specific points, but it doesn't scale to a whole state by hand.

**4. Crowdsourced (OpenStreetMap / OFDS)** — already confirmed too sparse in the US to lean on, but worth a real Overpass query rather than my earlier sparse-tag check, since coverage may exist unevenly by city.

Of these, #2 (least-cost-path along real corridors, from your existing endpoint data) is the one I'd actually recommend building — it's honest about being modeled rather than surveyed, and I can implement it directly in QGIS right now if you want. #1 is the one with the best shot at *actual* data for specific missing states, just slower (real records requests, not something I can do in this session). Want me to build the least-cost-path layer, or start drafting records requests for a few of the gap states?

content.text:
Let's do the records request first (quick, low-risk, and genuinely useful regardless of what happens with the GIS work), then start the least-cost-path build on Virginia as the test case.

## Virginia public records request (draft)

Virginia already has real data for Southside (MBC), but nothing for the rest of the state. The right target is VDOT, since every DOT-sourced win so far (AZ, UT, KY, IL) came from the same kind of internal permit/conduit inventory — that's the pattern worth testing here. Virginia's FOIA (Va. Code §2.2-3700 et seq.) covers this, and requests can be filed by any citizen with no stated reason required.

---

*To: VDOT FOIA Officer / Virginia Department of Transportation*
*Re: Freedom of Information Act Request — Fiber Optic Conduit / Utility Permit GIS Data*

Under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (Va. Code § 2.2-3700 et seq.), I am requesting the following record:

Any GIS dataset (shapefile, geodatabase, or ArcGIS REST service export) maintained by VDOT showing fiber optic cable or conduit routes within Virginia highway rights-of-way — whether compiled for utility permit tracking, dig-once coordination, or right-of-way management purposes. If this is organized by district (as some states' equivalent datasets are), I would appreciate either a statewide compilation or the individual district files.

If any portion of this record is exempt from disclosure, please provide the remainder and identify the specific statutory exemption(s) applied to the withheld portion, per § 2.2-3704(B).

I am requesting this in electronic format where available. Please let me know if any fees apply before proceeding.

---

That's ready to send as-is (via VDOT's FOIA contact — I didn't submit anything, this is a draft for you to review, add your name/contact info to, and send yourself). Want me to look up VDOT's actual FOIA submission address/portal to append?

Now starting the least-cost-path build for Virginia — pulling in real highway/rail corridor data and your existing endpoint layers.

content.text:
Good moment to clarify, since this distinction matters a lot for how this gets used:

**The points are real, verified locations** — 182 operating data centers (your existing FracTracker layer), 9 Internet2 sites, and 1 cable landing station (Virginia Beach), all filtered to Virginia. These aren't modeled or inferred — they're actual places where real data infrastructure exists, same as everything else already in your project.

**The lines are NOT real fiber routes — they're a computed guess.** Each line is the *shortest path* from one of those points to a hub I picked (Ashburn, VA — "Data Center Alley," which Internet2 itself treats as a real site, so it's a defensible anchor), computed by routing along the real highway and railway network (the 15,144 Interstate segments + 19,216 rail segments I just pulled from OpenStreetMap). The logic: fiber is overwhelmingly buried along existing rights-of-way because that's legally/economically how it gets built, so "shortest path along highways/rail" is a reasonable *proxy* for where a cable probably runs — but it's an inference, not a survey. No one confirmed a cable is actually on that exact path.

This is the same technique the one credible academic paper in this space (InterTubes) used when they couldn't get real carrier data either. It has to be labeled clearly as modeled/inferred wherever it appears — I'll keep it visually and semantically distinct from your real-route layers.

Checking the retry now — the first pass had a network topology bug (most routes came back null), just fixed with a snapping tolerance. Let me verify this one actually worked before finalizing anything.
